posts.title: MOOWR in plain words: manufacturing in a bonded warehouse
posts.excerpt: What the scheme lets a manufacturer defer, and what it asks in return.
posts.body:
MOOWR stands for Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations, 2019. It is made under section 65 of the Customs Act, 1962.

In short, a manufacturer can bring capital goods and raw materials into a licensed bonded warehouse without paying customs duty at that stage. Duty is paid when the finished goods or inputs leave the warehouse for sale in India. Goods exported are not charged import duty.

## What it helps with

- Cash flow, because duty on capital goods and inputs is deferred.
- Duty planning, because the point at which duty is paid depends on how goods leave the warehouse.
- Export-oriented units that want to avoid paying duty and claiming it back.

## What it asks of you

- A warehouse licence and a bond with the jurisdictional customs authority.
- Records of every item that comes in, is used and goes out, kept in the form customs expects.
- Ongoing compliance with the conditions of the licence, including how waste and scrap are treated.

Whether the scheme suits a business depends on its product, its sales mix between domestic and export, and its record-keeping. If you are weighing it, write to me with a short description of your operation.

posts.title: SCOMET: does your product need an export authorisation?
posts.excerpt: A short guide to the list, and why classification comes first.
posts.body:
SCOMET stands for Special Chemicals, Organisms, Materials, Equipment and Technologies. It is India's list of dual-use and strategic items whose export is controlled under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992.

The list sits in Appendix 3 to Schedule 2 of the ITC (HS) classifications and is updated from time to time through DGFT notifications. An item on the list needs an export authorisation before it ships. This can apply to goods, software and technology.

## Start with classification

The first step is to compare your product's technical specification with the entries on the current list. A product can fall under a category because of what it does, not what it is called. The same product may also be controlled only above a certain specification.

## Then check the end use and the destination

Even when an item is not listed, a catch-all provision can apply if the exporter knows the goods are meant for a prohibited end use. Keep your reasoning in writing.

If you are unsure, send me the product's technical data sheet and I will tell you what to check next.

posts.title: MOOWR in simple words: pay customs duty later, not at the port
posts.excerpt: A plain explanation of the scheme, with an example, for anyone who imports and manufactures in India.
posts.body:
Normally, when you bring goods into India, you pay customs duty at the port before you can take them out. For a factory that imports machines or raw materials, that is a large amount of cash paid long before any product is made or sold.

MOOWR is a scheme that lets you pay that duty later. The name stands for Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations, 2019. It works under section 65 of the Customs Act, 1962.

## The idea in one line

You keep your imported goods in a customs-approved warehouse (a bonded warehouse), do your manufacturing there, and pay duty only when the goods leave for sale in India.

## A simple example

A company imports a machine and some raw material. Without the scheme, it pays duty on both at the port, then waits months to earn money from the product. With the scheme, the goods go into the bonded warehouse without duty at that stage. The company makes its product. If it sells in India, duty is paid when the goods leave the warehouse. If it exports, no import duty is charged on the imported goods used.

## Who it helps

- Factories that import machinery or raw materials
- Businesses that export a large part of what they make
- Businesses that want to keep cash for running the business instead of locking it in duty

## What you need to do

- Apply to the customs authority for permission and a licence for the warehouse
- Give a bond, which is a written promise to follow the rules and pay any duty that falls due
- Keep clear records of what comes in, what is used, what is made, and what goes out
- Send the returns and records that customs asks for, on time

## Things to think about first

- Duty is put off, not removed. Goods sold in India will still attract duty.
- The records are the heart of the scheme. Poor records can cause trouble later.
- The rules and how customs applies them change from time to time, so check the current position before you apply.
- It does not suit every business. It depends on what you import, what you make, and how much you sell in India and abroad.

## Is it right for you?

If you import machines or materials and want to ease your cash flow, it is worth a look. Send me a short note about your business: what you import, what you make, and where you sell. I will tell you whether MOOWR is worth considering and what the next steps would be.

This post is general information, not advice on your particular case.
